newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU leaders to ponder IGC progress.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders to ponder IGC progress.

text.p: When European Union leaders sit down in Dublin this week to review progress in talks on a new EU treaty, they will find that a rough outline of what is likely to emerge is available but that little else has been agreed.
The question is whether this is normal, six months into what is slated to be 15 months of negotiations, or whether it is a sign of stagnation and pending crisis.
Heads of state and government from the 15 EU countries are to meet in the Irish capital on Saturday for an informal chat about the EU's preparations for the next century.
At issue is the state of the inter-governmental conference (IGC) designed to get the EU in shape to handle an influx of new members from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean.
The talks began in March, and have generally followed a plan laid out first by the Italians, who held the EU presidency until June, and then by the Irish, who took over.
This has entailed systematic discussions of various areas to be covered by the review, collecting countries' views, and recently, drafting potential treaty language.
But no firm agreements have been reached -- only what Dutch European Affairs Minister Michiel Patijn, one of the negotiators, calls "the contours" of a future treaty.
"If you schedule a conference for 15 months, you can't expect (too much progress) after six," Patijn told Reuters in a recent interview.
Most negotiators expect a frienzied phase of horse-trading next year just before the IGC's scheduled end.
But others have become stingingly critical of the pace of the talks, charging that the IGC has got nowhere and needs a big boost from the EU leaders on Saturday.

"We have spent over a year going around in circles like whirling dervishes...and we have not made even half a centimetre of progress," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Sunday. He was including preparatory talks in his time frame.
What the leaders will find on Saturday is that the areas that the new treaty will likely touch have been identified, but that specific pacts remain a long way off.
The new treaty is widely expected to include a so-called employment chapter, designed to put job creation at the top of the EU's agenda. This is supported by a majority of states, negotiators say.

It is also likely to build on previous pledges to create a strong Common Foreign and Security Policy. There is widespread support for creating a new forward planning unit and appointing some kind of senior figure as coordinator.
There is also general acceptance that EU institutions and procedures will have to be changed to accommodate new members.
But there is no agreement on how this is to be done, with Britain, in particular, holding out against any loss of sovereignty in the name of efficiency.
Small countries are also fighting moves to cut the number of EU commissioners or their own role as EU presidents.
Overall, negotiators say, the most significant new proposal may be to incorporate "flexibility" into the treaty -- a concept allowing some countries to integrate faster or deeper than others.
"Flexibility may suit those who want to press ahead, and it may suit those who do not want to join them," Irish negotiator Noel Dorr said.
